checkpoints: Không đồng ý với đề xuất của đồng nghiệp — DO Managed Database không có parameter group nhiều tùy chọn kiểu AWS RDS để tự do chỉnh max_connections
Dù có chỉnh được thì mở 5000 kết nối trực tiếp cũng tốn quá nhiều RAM, đủ làm crash một node nhỏ (mỗi kết nối Postgres tốn khoảng 10MB RAM)
Giải pháp đúng trên DO là dùng digitalocean_database_connection_pool — PgBouncer chạy ở cổng 25061, gộp hàng nghìn client vào một số lượng kết nối thật tới Postgres nhỏ hơn nhiều (tham số size)
Cho production nên chọn mode = "transaction" — trả kết nối về pool ngay sau mỗi commit, tiết kiệm kết nối nhất
Phân biệt đúng các mode pooling còn lại: session giữ kết nối suốt cả phiên (kém hiệu quả hơn transaction), statement trả kết nối ngay sau mỗi statement (nghiêm ngặt nhất)
Lưu ý quan trọng nhất: theo Registry, connection pool chỉ hỗ trợ PostgreSQL — nếu backend dùng MySQL, DO không có PgBouncer tương đương built-in, phải tự chạy pooler ngoài như ProxySQL

Không có "IAM policy" nào để viết ở DO Managed Database — access control không phải là 1 policy document gắn vào cluster kiểu AWS RDS + IAM, mà là 3 lớp cơ chế tách biệt (DB user, firewall, network isolation).

Lớp DB user: tạo 1 digitalocean_database_user riêng cho service (role tự động "normal", không phải "primary" như doadmin), app code chỉ được kết nối bằng user riêng đó, tuyệt đối không dùng doadmin mặc định.

Lớp firewall trusted-source: cluster public theo mặc định, nên phải thêm digitalocean_database_firewall để chỉ cho phép đúng nguồn cần kết nối (1 Droplet cụ thể, 1 tag, hoặc App Platform app qua rule.type = "app").
Firewall chặn ở network layer, trước khi request chạm tới Postgres auth — đây là kiểm soát theo nguồn kết nối (network-level), khác với kiểm soát theo credential ở lớp DB user.
Lớp network isolation: nếu cần cô lập mạng hoàn toàn, set private_network_uuid trỏ vào 1 VPC để cluster chỉ reachable qua private_host, không bao giờ lộ ra internet công cộng.

Ba lớp này gộp lại chính là ý nghĩa của "least-privilege" trên DO: kiểm soát nằm rải rác trong nhiều resource Terraform (user/firewall/VPC), không có 1 JSON policy tập trung nào để review qua PR như cách AWS IAM hoạt động.
The investigation should start from the switch to PgBouncer's `mode = "transaction"` pool, since that's exactly when the errors began.
Root cause: the JDBC driver via Hibernate caches prepared statements per session, assuming a statement prepared once can be reused for the whole session.

In `mode = "transaction"`, PgBouncer returns the real Postgres connection to the pool right after every commit, so the next statement in the same application-side session can get routed to a different physical Postgres connection where that statement was never PREPARE-d.
This is unlike `mode = "session"`, where a client holds exactly one Postgres connection for its entire session lifetime, so the prepared statement cache never gets out of sync.
However, `mode = "session"` is less efficient than transaction mode because Postgres connections are reused less across different clients.

The fix that keeps transaction mode's performance is adding `prepareThreshold=0` to the JDBC connection string, forcing the PostgreSQL driver to stop using server-side prepared statements entirely (falling back to client-side/simple query), removing the cache layer causing the mismatch.
Verify by rerunning the exact business flow that used to throw the error across a few hundred consecutive requests and confirming there are no more `prepared statement ... does not exist` errors.
Also verify by measuring latency to make sure the increase from losing server-side prepare is acceptable.
Identifies that the Terraform provisions no `digitalocean_database_firewall` for the cluster at all — no network restriction exists in the diff.

Explains why that's a live risk today, not theoretical: DigitalOcean Managed Databases are publicly reachable by default, so right now the cluster accepts connection attempts from any IP on the internet as long as credentials match (real brute-force surface).
Identifies that the app authenticates as `doadmin` — the cluster's built-in `primary`-role (highest-privilege) user — instead of a dedicated per-service account.
Explains the blast-radius consequence: because `doadmin` holds primary/cluster-wide privileges, leaking that one credential compromises the entire cluster, not just the `orders` service's own data.
Identifies that the `connection_uri` output is declared with `sensitive = false`, so Terraform prints the full URI — including the password — into plan/apply output and CLI logs.

Prescribes the firewall fix at the correct precision: add a `digitalocean_database_firewall` rule scoped to the minimal needed source (a `tag` or `app` reference), and explicitly calls out that a bare hardcoded IP is the wrong scope.
Prescribes the user fix at the correct precision: provision a dedicated `digitalocean_database_user` (e.g. `orders_app`) with role `normal`, and repoint `.env.production` to it instead of `doadmin`.

Names a concrete way to verify the fixes actually took effect post-apply — e.g. `doctl databases firewalls list` / `user list` showing the new rule and user, or confirming a connection attempt from outside the allowed source is rejected at the network layer before reaching Mongo auth.

cleanup_policy = "compact" is wrong for this use case: it keeps only the latest record per key (correct for changelog/materialized state), but "order placed" is an event stream where every order is a distinct event that billing/email/inventory all need to read in full — compact would silently drop older events whenever they share a key.
retention_ms = "-1" means no time limit on retention, directly contradicting the 7-day deletion requirement and causing the topic to grow unboundedly.
Fix: switch cleanup_policy to "delete", matching event-stream semantics of retain-by-time-then-delete.
Fix: set retention_ms to "604800000" (7 days = 7×24×60×60×1000 ms) instead of "-1".
retention_bytes can stay at "-1" since only a time limit is wanted here, not a size cap.
Verify with doctl that the topic remains state = active after applying the change.
Verify by monitoring over more than 7 days that old messages auto-expire without manual intervention.
Verify by testing that a newly joined consumer can read exactly the last 7 days of history before catching up to live.

DB_HOST is injected as an env var with `type = "GENERAL"` (value from `digitalocean_database_cluster.main.private_host`, `scope = "RUN_TIME"`) since the host isn't sensitive and can appear plainly in App Spec/UI/state.

DB_PASSWORD is injected as an env var with `type = "SECRET"` (value from `digitalocean_database_user.app.password`) — DO encrypts the value at rest and hides it from logs/UI, showing `EV[1:...]` instead of plaintext.

A `digitalocean_database_firewall` resource restricts access with `rule.type = "app"` and `value = digitalocean_app.main.id`, instead of a hardcoded IP (which changes on scaling) or public exposure, so only this exact app can connect to the database at the network layer.

This is explicitly NOT a secrets manager like AWS Secrets Manager/GCP Secret Manager — `SECRET` is just an App Spec field-level protection (as configured above), not a dedicated secrets-management service.
There is no versioning or rotation policy for the secret — you cannot roll back to an old value, and rotating it means manually re-running `terraform apply`.
There is no IAM-grant per-secret — no runtime `GetSecretValue` call exists, and there's no way to grant which app can read which secret.

The password value from `digitalocean_database_user.app.password` still sits plaintext in the Terraform state, so the state itself must be protected with an encrypted remote backend the same way you'd protect the secret.

Verification: `doctl apps spec get <app-id>` should show `DB_HOST` as plaintext but `DB_PASSWORD` masked as `EV[1:...]`, and `doctl databases firewalls list <cluster-id>` should show exactly one `type=app` rule pointing at the app id, with no broader `ip_addr` rules.
States plainly that a read replica does NOT save this situation — the missing data is not recoverable from it.

Explains the mechanism: the replica uses async streaming replication that faithfully applies the same operations (including the bad DELETE), so the same ~80% data loss happens on the replica too, only lagging by milliseconds to seconds.
Correctly frames the read replica's real purpose: read scaling only — explicitly NOT a high-availability mechanism and NOT a backup.

Correctly frames the HA standby's real purpose: synchronous auto-failover for availability when the primary dies — but it does not serve read queries and does not protect against logical errors since it applies the same bad command too.
Identifies PITR/snapshot as the actual backup, independent of both the read replica and the HA standby, usable to restore to a point in the past.
States the correct recovery target: restore into a NEW cluster at the point in time right before the DELETE ran — never restore on top of the live production cluster.

States a verification step before cutover: check the new cluster's data (e.g. row counts on orders, spot-check a few critical records) before deciding to redirect traffic or merge back the missing data.
Names at least one concrete preventive measure: a review/dry-run/transaction-rollback discipline for prod DELETE/UPDATE, and/or periodically testing PITR restores in staging.

GCP không cho "attach một policy vào identity" theo kiểu AWS IAM; chiều gắn ngược nhau giữa hai nền tảng: AWS gắn policy VÀO identity (permission đi theo user/role khi di chuyển), còn GCP gắn role và member VÀO resource — permission "sống" ở phía resource chứ không phải phía identity.
Model thật của GCP: IAM policy của một resource (project/folder/organization) là một danh sách các binding, mỗi binding là cặp (role, một hoặc nhiều member).
Policy được kế thừa xuôi theo cấp bậc: organization → folder → project → resource.
Effective permission thật sự của một member là UNION của mọi binding áp dụng cho nó ở MỌI cấp, không chỉ binding tại cấp đang xem.

Hệ quả thực tế: để biết chính xác một service account có thể làm gì, không thể chỉ đọc IAM policy của project — phải kiểm tra cả folder và organization phía trên, vì một binding ở cấp cao hơn có thể âm thầm cấp thêm quyền mà người review chỉ nhìn ở project sẽ không thấy.

Disagree with granting `roles/editor` — it's a basic role, broad in scope (near-full create/update/delete rights on most project resources), which directly conflicts with the stated need of only list/get.
This is a severe least-privilege violation: if the service account leaks or is compromised, an attacker could modify or delete nearly everything in the project.

GCP has three role types in order of preference: basic (owner/editor/viewer — only appropriate for personal sandboxes), predefined (Google-maintained, scoped to a single service, generally the preferred choice), and custom (you enumerate the exact permissions yourself, used when predefined is still broader than needed).
Recommend trying predefined roles first — `roles/compute.viewer` + `roles/storage.objectViewer` — since they map closely to the required list/get actions.
Caveat: verify whether those predefined roles match exactly or still include excess permissions beyond plain list/get, since predefined roles can be slightly broader than the stated need.

If predefined roles are still too broad, create a custom role (e.g. via `google_project_iam_custom_role`) listing exactly the needed permissions: `compute.instances.list`, `compute.instances.get`, `storage.objects.list`.
Trade-off of a custom role: you must maintain it yourself as Google adds, removes, or deprecates permissions, whereas predefined roles are updated automatically by Google.
Disagree with the teammate's suggestion — creating two separate VPCs and peering them is not the correct approach on GCP.

Identifies the root cause of the mistake: the suggestion carries over AWS's mental model, where `aws_vpc` is bound to a single region, so multi-region connectivity on AWS needs VPC peering or a Transit Gateway.
States that on GCP a VPC (`google_compute_network`) is a global resource — it has no `region` argument and spans every region in the world.
Correct architecture starts with just ONE custom-mode VPC.
Add two `google_compute_subnetwork` resources under that same VPC — one subnet in `us-central1`, one in `asia-southeast1` — each with its `network` field pointing to the same VPC.

Two subnets in different regions within the same VPC automatically communicate cross-region over the Google backbone, with no peering resource declared at all — this is exactly the 'global network' advantage that creating multiple VPCs and peering would throw away.
The two subnets must still have non-overlapping `ip_cidr_range`s even though they share one VPC, since GCP refuses to create an overlapping one — so CIDR must be planned disjoint from the start.
